column5: straight road to a settled city
column6: The commentary hears ihdinā as a request to reach the home at the path's end; these desert wanderers are led by YHWH on a straight route until they reach an inhabited city.
The commentary says ihdinā asks to be brought beyond the road toward its home; this speaker asks light and truth to guide him and bring him to God's holy mountain and dwelling.
The commentary's hedy animal reaches the House; Deuteronomy sends burnt offerings and other gifts to the place YHWH chooses to establish his name.
The commentary describes an animal carried to the Haram for offering; Leviticus requires Israelites to bring oxen, lambs, or goats to the tent entrance as offerings to YHWH.
The commentary connects mawsim with a gathering and the House; here tribes go up to Jerusalem as Israel's testimony to give thanks to YHWH's name.
The commentary's mawsim is a marked season of gathering; Exodus fixes an appointed feast and says no one should appear before God empty-handed.

The commentary labels bismi with Arabic roots s-m-w and w-s-m and says the uttered name raises remembrance of its bearer; Hebrew shem is remembered at an altar where burnt and peace offerings are made.

column5: God's name placed on a people
column6: The commentary says God's name is spoken over the hedy animal; this priestly formula places YHWH's name over Israel and promises blessing, applying the ritual name to the protected community.

column5: call on a god's name at a bull altar
column6: The commentary joins the offered animal with the name spoken over it; at Carmel, two bulls are prepared and each side calls on its god's name, in a test that contrasts YHWH with Baal.
The commentary brings the hedy offering together with God's name and the worlds; Malachi pictures nations from sunrise to sunset offering incense and a pure gift to YHWH's name.

column5: ram offered instead of a son
column6: The commentary's hedy is an animal carried to a sacred destination; Abraham offers a ram as a burnt offering instead of Isaac, making the animal a substitute for a beloved child.
The commentary reads h-d-y as a bride conducted to her husband's home; this royal wedding psalm says the princess is led to the king with companions following her.
The commentary's bride is brought to her husband's house; the next wedding verse has the bridal party enter the king's palace with joy.
The commentary says the spoken name raises remembrance of the named one; this wedding psalm promises that the king's name will be remembered through generations.

column5: bride brought to the husband's tent
column6: The commentary describes the bride being taken to her husband's home; Isaac brings Rebekah into his mother's tent and takes her as his wife.

column5: leaving one household to join another
column6: The commentary's bride is gathered to her husband; Genesis describes the marital bond as leaving father and mother and cleaving to one's wife.

column5: bride directed to her husband's family home
column6: The commentary's bride is conveyed to her husband's house; Raguel gives Sarah to Tobias and directs him to take her to his father's house. Tobit's verse numbering varies among editions.

The commentary places marriage before the bride's journey; this mishna frames betrothal as a legal act through money, document, or intercourse, clarifying the formal bond preceding full household union.
The commentary says the Qur'anic queen's gift to Solomon fails to reach him; Kings narrates the same queen giving him abundant gold, spices, and stones as a successful royal exchange.
The commentary's Sheba scene ends with Solomon dismissing the gift; Kings says he gave the queen whatever she desired and royal gifts in return.

column5: Queen of the South as witness
column6: The commentary's Queen of Sheba sends Solomon a gift that he rejects; Matthew remembers her journey from earth's ends to hear Solomon and makes her a witness against Jesus' generation, adding a judgment interpretation.
The commentary says a gift sent to a rival does not reach Solomon; Abigail's gift reaches David, who accepts it and abandons his plan to kill Nabal's household.
The commentary's petitioner seeks a group's protection and a safe destination; Numbers appoints cities to which an accidental killer may flee from the blood-avenger.

column5: a place of refuge for accidental killing
column6: The commentary describes a person accepted under protection; Exodus says God provides a place to which the unintended killer may flee.
The commentary calls the petitioner inviolable like the House's offering; Exodus orders even an intentional killer taken from God's altar and put to death, defining a limit to sanctuary protection.
The commentary's refugee asks a group for protection or a pledge; Rahab asks the Israelite spies to swear that they will spare her family because she has shown them loyalty.
The commentary links refuge with a protective covenant; the spies swear to preserve Rahab's life if she keeps their mission secret.
The commentary's petitioner asks a group for protection and a pledge; the Egyptian slave asks David to swear not to kill or return him before he agrees to guide the pursuit.
The commentary says a person who seeks a group's protection becomes inviolable like the House's offering; Joab flees to YHWH's altar and grips its horns for sanctuary.

column5: altar refuge does not save Joab
column6: The commentary presents the asylum seeker as protected like a sacred offering; after Joab takes refuge at the altar, Solomon's men execute him, showing that this sanctuary's protection can fail.
The commentary describes an outsider seeking a group's safe protection; Boaz blesses Ruth for coming to take refuge under YHWH's wings.
The commentary develops refuge and a bride brought to her husband's home; Ruth first seeks refuge as a foreigner, then marries Boaz and joins his household.
The commentary glosses Arabic ʿibāda as obedience and service; Deuteronomy uses the Hebrew cognate ʿābad for serving YHWH, alongside cleaving to him and swearing by his name.

The commentary labels Arabic rabb as Lord but also reports a separate covenant sense; Daniel's Aramaic rab names Daniel chief of the governors, supporting the rank or master sense rather than the covenant gloss.
The commentary's Arabic malik names God as sovereign; the Hebrew cognate melekh here declares God king over all the earth, while the commentary's marriage gloss remains a separate Arabic branch.
The commentary pictures guidance whose path ends at a sacred home; Isaiah has peoples go up to YHWH's mountain to learn his ways and walk in his paths.
The commentary's worshippers ask God to guide them along a straight path; Isaiah instead commands a wilderness voice to prepare a straight highway for YHWH's own coming.

column5: a star guides travelers to a house
column6: The commentary says guidance carries its subject to a destination; the Magi follow the star until it stands over the place where the child is.

column5: gift delivered to a child in a house
column6: The commentary describes a gift carried to its recipient and contrasts the rejected gift to Solomon; the Magi enter a house, worship the child, and present him gifts that are received.
The commentary describes a petitioner seeking protection and a safe destination; Joseph takes the child and mother to Egypt to escape Herod's threat.
The commentary's hedy animal is carried from a flock toward the House; Jesus' parable has a shepherd carry a recovered sheep on his shoulders, turning the journey into rescue rather than sacrifice.
The commentary hears ihdinā as a road that reaches home; the shepherd returns with the sheep and calls friends and neighbors together to celebrate.
The commentary's ihdinā asks to be led on a path; Zechariah says the dawn from on high will guide people's feet into the way of peace.

column5: sheep called by name and led
column6: The commentary says God's name is uttered over the hedy and the animal is taken toward its destination; Jesus' shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, though here the sheep are living followers.
The commentary says the guided path has a house at its end; Jesus promises his disciples many dwelling places in his Father's house.

column5: the guide takes people to himself
column6: The commentary's bride reaches her husband's home and the refugee his safe place; Jesus promises to come and take his followers to himself so they can be where he is.

column5: worship no longer tied to either mountain
column6: The commentary follows the hedy to the Haram and the old House; Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour comes when worship will be neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem.

The commentary locates the sacrificial animal's destination at a sacred House; Jesus describes the coming worship as in spirit and truth, shifting attention from a sanctuary site to the worshippers' manner.

column5: the path is prepared for the Lord
column6: The commentary's prayer asks God to guide worshippers on the straight way; Mark applies Isaiah's road formula to John preparing the Lord's way, reversing who is guided and who comes.

column5: a traveler asks for a guide
column6: The commentary's ihdinā is a request for guidance; the Ethiopian traveler asks how he can understand Isaiah unless someone guides him, and Philip joins him on the road.

The commentary's hedy is an animal led to a sacred destination; Acts quotes Isaiah's sheep led to slaughter in Philip's explanation of Jesus, making the sacrificial animal a Christian reading of a human figure.

The commentary defines a gift as kindness sent to someone loved and the hedy as an offering for nearness to God; Ephesians says Christ loved people and gave himself as an offering and sacrifice to God.

column5: the bride presented to the husband
column6: The commentary says the bride is gathered to her husband; Ephesians reads marriage as Christ presenting the church to himself, a Christian interpretation that turns the household image into Christ and church.
The commentary's asylum seeker asks a group for shelter or a pledge; Hebrews describes people who fled for refuge to seize hope grounded in God's unchangeable promise and oath.
The commentary's hedy is brought to the House as an offering; Hebrews describes sacrificial animals whose blood the high priest brings into the holy place while their bodies are burned outside camp.
The commentary's animal reaches the sacred House; Hebrews says Jesus suffered outside the city gate and sanctified people by his blood, relocating the Christian sacrifice beyond the city.

column5: the community as a spiritual house
column6: The commentary describes livestock brought to a House for worship; Peter calls believers living stones in a spiritual house who offer spiritual sacrifices, interpreting sanctuary and offering through a community.
The commentary describes a gift as kindness sent to someone loved; Paul calls the Philippians' material gift a fragrant offering and acceptable sacrifice to God.
The commentary joins the hedy animal with the request for guidance toward a safe destination; Revelation's Lamb becomes shepherd and guides the protected multitude to springs of living water.

The commentary labels Arabic rabb as Lord and reports a covenant-related branch; Mary calls the risen Jesus Rabbouni, an Aramaic honorific meaning teacher or master, supporting the address sense rather than covenant.
The commentary itself labels Arabic anʿamta, favor, and anʿām, herds, under n-ʿ-m; Hebrew noam here means YHWH's gracious pleasantness, a possible cognate for the favor sense but not for livestock.
